Distribution Function of the Modified Half-Normal Distribution

Source: R/pmhn.R
pmhn.Rd

Computes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the Modified Half-Normal (MHN) distribution with parameters alpha, beta, and gamma.

Usage

pmhn(q, alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

Arguments

q

Numeric vector of quantiles.

alpha

Shape parameter (\(\alpha > 0\)). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

beta

Rate-type parameter (\(\beta > 0\)), the coefficient of the Gaussian tail \(\exp(-\beta x^2)\); larger values pull mass toward zero. Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

gamma

Tilt parameter (\(\gamma \in R\)), the coefficient of the exponential tilt \(\exp(\gamma x)\). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 0.

lower.tail

Logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(X \le q)\), otherwise \(P(X > q)\).

log.p

Logical; if TRUE, probabilities are returned on the log scale. Default: FALSE. Both flags are read with as.logical(), so that 1 is TRUE; a value that gives NA is an error.

Value

A numeric vector. The output length equals max(length(q), length(alpha), length(beta), length(gamma)), or 0 if any of them has length zero; each input is recycled to that length following standard R recycling rules. For q <= 0 the CDF is 0; for q = Inf it is 1. As in pgamma, an element whose parameters lie outside the parameter space (alpha or beta not positive and finite, or gamma not finite) is NaN, with a warning, and an element with an NA or NaN among its inputs is NA or NaN (NA if any of them is NA), without one; the other elements are unaffected. The arguments must be numeric (double, integer or logical): a factor, a character string, a complex number, a list or NULL is an error, as in pnorm. As with pnorm, the attributes of q (names, dim, dimnames) are kept when the result has the length of q; a classed q, such as a Date, is taken as its numbers and gives a plain vector. Unlike pnorm, attributes of a longer parameter vector are not carried over.

Details

In the general case the lower tail is computed, over the part of the parameter space given below, from the series representation $$F(x \mid \alpha, \beta, \gamma) = \frac{1}{\Psi[\alpha/2, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}]} \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \frac{z^i}{i!}\, \Gamma(s_i)\, P(s_i, \beta x^2)$$ where \(z = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\), \(s_i = (\alpha + i)/2\), and \(P(s, y)\) is the regularized lower incomplete gamma function (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 1b: there each term \(2\beta^{\alpha/2}\gamma^i\beta^{-(\alpha+i)/2}/(2\, i!)\) reduces to \(z^i/i!\), and \(\Gamma(s)\, P(s, y) = \gamma(s, y)\), where \(\gamma(s, y)\) is the lower incomplete gamma function used in the paper). The infinite sum is truncated at an upper bound on the length \(K = \max\{K_1, K_2\}\) of Sun et al. (2023), Supplementary Lemma 10(d), from the geometric decay of the terms that Lemma 10(a, b) establish, which makes the truncation residual bounded by the working tolerance sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) divided by \(\Psi\); for \(\gamma > 0\), where every term is positive, it is truncated earlier where that bound is below the rounding of the sum, so that the residual is below the larger of that and \(2^{-53} F\). The series is tried first for \(\alpha < 1\) at every tilt up to \(z = 1000\), and for \(\alpha \ge 1\) only where \(|z| \le 20\) and \(\alpha \le 100\). There a numerical integration of the density on \([0, q]\) replaces it where, for \(\gamma < 0\), the rounding of the alternating terms, set against the cancellation between them, could make its relative error exceed sqrt(.Machine$double.eps); where it would need more than \(10^6\) terms, which happens for \(|z|\) above about 830, and so only for \(\alpha < 1\); and where \(\beta q^2\) is below the smallest normal double. Elsewhere, outside the ranges measured from the peak (see below), the integration is used directly, being the faster of the two there. It is Gauss-Kronrod for \(\alpha \ge 1\), and for \(\alpha < 1\), where the density is unbounded at the origin, a closed form next to the origin, then tanh-sinh up to \(q\) or up to the interior peak that a positive tilt can give the density, whichever comes first, and Gauss-Kronrod past that peak. For \(z > 1000\) the integral and \(\Psi\) are both taken with \(\gamma^2/(4\beta)\) removed from their logarithms, which are otherwise too large for their difference to be accurate.

The upper tail \(P(X > q)\) is computed directly, by Gauss-Kronrod quadrature of the density over \((q, \infty)\) on a logarithmic axis, and not as \(1 - F\), which would round to 0 once it falls below about \(10^{-16}\). Each tail is computed directly on its own side of the peak of the density of \(\log X\), the positive root of \(2\beta x^2 - \gamma x - \alpha = 0\), which lies at or above the median; above it the lower tail is returned as one minus the upper tail. With log.p = TRUE both tails are formed on the log scale throughout, so that \(\log F\) is still resolved where \(F\) rounds to 1 or is below the smallest positive double. At or below the median \(\log P(X > q)\) is about \(-F\), and the logarithm of the quadrature carries an absolute error of about \(\epsilon\) times the size of the terms it is assembled from, \(|\log\Psi| + (\alpha/2)|\log\beta| + m(1 + |\log v^*|)\) (\(m\) and \(v^*\) as in Range), with \(\gamma^2/(4\beta)\) removed from \(\log\Psi\) for \(z > 1000\), as in the quadratures. Wherever that could pass \(10^{-9}\) of \(F\), it is formed instead as \(\log(1 - F)\) from \(\log F\), which keeps the relative accuracy of \(F\): for parameters of order one only below \(F\) of about \(10^{-5}\). For \(\alpha < 1\) with \(|z| > 20\), where the series costs milliseconds, \(F\) is taken for this from the numerical integration wherever that agrees with the upper tail to within the error of the latter. The lower tail has the matching switch. Below that peak \(F\) can still exceed one half, and for a small shape it is close to 1 over most of the range below the peak, one less a tail proportional to \(\alpha\). There \(\log F\), about \(-P(X > q)\), is assembled from terms of the size of \(\log\Psi\), \((\alpha/2)\log\beta\) and \((\alpha - 1)\log q\) that cancel, and carries an absolute error of about \(\epsilon\) times their size. Wherever that could pass \(10^{-9}\) of \(\log F\) and the error of the upper tail, carried into \(\log F\), is estimated at less than half as much, it is formed instead as \(\log(1 - P(X > q))\) from the upper tail, which keeps the relative accuracy of \(P(X > q)\). Without that switch the error would pass \(10^{-9}\) of \(\log F\) for a shape below about \(10^{-6}\) under a small tilt, and below a smaller shape under a large one. A subnormal shape, below the smallest normal double, is served apart (see dmhn), and there \(\log F\) keeps its relative accuracy too.

At \(\gamma = 0\) and at \(\alpha = 1\) exactly the distribution function is computed from the law it reduces to; a shape or a tilt merely close to those values is a different law, and is computed as in the general case:

  • \(\gamma = 0\): \(F(q) = P(\alpha/2, \beta q^2)\), the regularized incomplete gamma function of the square-root-Gamma law (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6a), by pgamma, or as its leading term \((\beta q^2)^{\alpha/2} / \Gamma(\alpha/2 + 1)\), exact to double precision, where \(\beta q^2\) is below the smallest normal double; for \(\alpha \le 10^6\). Above it the Gamma law is so narrow that rounding \(\beta q^2\) moves it by a visible part of its width (up to about \(10^{-6}\) of \(F\) at \(\alpha = 10^{20}\)), and \(\gamma = 0\) is measured from the peak as below.

  • \(\alpha = 1\): the truncated-normal CDF (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6b), by pnorm, or through the scaled complementary error function where the truncation point 0 lies three or more standard deviations above the mean \(\gamma/(2\beta)\) of the untruncated normal, \(-\gamma/\sqrt{2\beta} \ge 3\). Near the truncation point the lower tail is summed from a short series, so that it keeps its relative accuracy however small it is.

For a shape \(\alpha\) or a scale-free tilt \(z = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) above \(10^6\), and wherever the terms of the ordinary forms grow too large (see Range), both tails are measured from the peak \(v^*\) of the density of \(\log X\), the positive root of \(2\beta x^2 - \gamma x - \alpha = 0\), in the variable \(w = \log(x/v^*)\): the tail on the side of \(\log(q/v^*)\) away from the peak is the integral of \(\exp(-\alpha(e^w - 1 - w) - \beta v^{*2}(e^w - 1)^2)\) over that side, taken by Gauss-Kronrod quadrature in offsets from q, over the same integral on the whole line, and the other tail is its complement. Nothing of the size of \(\alpha \log x\) or \(\gamma^2/(4\beta)\) is formed, whose rounding would otherwise leave the tails \(10^{-7}\) off at \(\alpha = 10^8\) and farther off as \(z\) grows, and no abscissa is rounded to the doubles next to the peak, which are a fraction \(z\,2^{-53}\) of the law's standard deviation apart. \(v^*\) is held as a double next to it plus its offset from that double.

Range. The ordinary forms are used only while the larger \(m\) of \(\alpha\) and \(z\) is at most \(10^6\) and \(m (1 + |\log v^*|)\), the size of their largest terms (\(\alpha \log x\), \((\alpha/2) \log\beta\), and the rounding of quadrature abscissae placed in \(\log x\)), is at most \(10^7\): at \(\beta = 1\) up to a shape of \(10^6\) or a tilt of about \(7.3 \times 10^5\), and at \(\beta = 10^{\pm 300}\) up to about \(3 \times 10^4\) for either. That keeps their error within 10 standard deviations of the peak below \(10^{-8}\); measured from the peak it is about \(10^{-14}\). Farther out in the upper tail the error of the ordinary forms grows with the distance from the peak, and close to that bound it reaches about \(3 \times 10^{-8}\) at 36 standard deviations, where the tail is of order \(10^{-284}\). So for \(\alpha \le 10^{15}\), \(|z| \le 10^{15}\) and \(\beta\) in \([10^{-300}, 10^{300}]\) both tails are accurate to the working tolerance sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) within 10 standard deviations of the peak, and to about twice that beyond. Outside that range the law can be narrower than the spacing of the doubles near its peak (for \(z\) above about \(10^{16}\), or \(\alpha\) above about \(10^{31}\)); the probabilities are then still those of the exact law at the doubles q given, a step from 0 to 1 between two adjacent doubles, whose value at the double nearest the peak is set by where the peak lies within its spacing. Two cases give NA with a warning instead: within 45 standard deviations of the peak of a law narrower than the spacing by a factor of order \(10^{19}\) (\(z\) beyond about \(10^{35}\), \(\alpha\) beyond about \(10^{70}\)), where the position of the peak cannot be resolved finely enough; and where the whole law lies beyond the largest double without a positive tilt to place it (a shape near the largest double against a subnormal \(\beta\)). A third case lies at the other end of the range: where \(\beta\) and the tilt are both close to the largest double (\(\beta\) from about \(2 \times 10^{307}\) with \(\gamma\) near the largest double, or from about \(5 \times 10^{307}\) with \(\gamma\) from about \(10^{306}\)), at points \(q\) above the peak where \(\beta q\) passes about half the largest double, the upper tail is NA with a warning or, with log.p = TRUE, -Inf where the log probability is finite. Where \(z\) itself overflows, the law is its limit: Gamma(\(\alpha\), rate \(|\gamma|\)) under a negative tilt, and normal about its mode with variance \(1/(2\beta)\) under a positive one. For \(\alpha = 1\) with the truncation point \(z_0 = -\gamma/\sqrt{2\beta}\) far beyond 3, the same forms hold up to \(z_0 = \infty\), where the law is Exponential with rate \(|\gamma|\); below \(-10^3\) the standardised offset is formed from \(2\beta q - \gamma\) in one rounding (as \(\beta q - \gamma/2\), so also where \(2\beta\) overflows), not from a rounded mean \(\gamma/(2\beta)\); the lower tail within \(|z_0|/2\) standard deviations of 0, where that offset is resolved only to about \(\epsilon |z_0|\) of one, is taken from the ratio of the two normal lower tails written with the exact distance \(q\sqrt{2\beta}\) from the truncation point.

When any of alpha, beta, gamma is a vector, the CDF is evaluated element-wise. The Fox-Wright \(\Psi\) normalizing constant is computed once for each position of the recycling cycle while that cycle is at most 256 long, and otherwise once for each run of consecutive elements that share the \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) triple. So recycled parameters, and parameter vectors in which equal triples are adjacent, are much faster than triples that alternate along a long vector, and than calling pmhn inside an R loop.

References

Sun, J., Kong, M., & Pal, S. (2023). The Modified-Half-Normal distribution: Properties and an efficient sampling scheme. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, 52(5), 1591–1613.

See also

dmhn, qmhn, rmhn

Examples

# Basic evaluation
pmhn(c(0.5, 1, 1.5), alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1)
#> [1] 0.1129101 0.4338796 0.7614259

# Tail / log forms
pmhn(2, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
#> [1] 0.06369619
pmhn(2, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1, log.p = TRUE)
#> [1] -0.06581527

# Special case: gamma = 0 reduces to sqrt-Gamma
all.equal(pmhn(1.5, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 0),
          pgamma(1.5^2, shape = 1, rate = 1))
#> [1] TRUE
